# Probability, simply {#sec-ch02}

You do not need advanced maths to use AI well. But you do need to read one kind of number correctly: a probability, such as "70% chance". This short chapter covers the only three ideas about probability that the rest of the book needs.

::: {.goals}
- Understand what "70% chance" really means.
- Avoid the most common trap: forgetting how rare something is.
- See, in plain words, how a machine learns a probability.
:::

## What "70% chance" means

Suppose the weather app says there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow, and it does not rain. Was the app wrong?

One day cannot tell us. Take all the days when the app said "70%". If it rained on about 70 out of every 100 such days, the app is doing its job. Tomorrow was simply one of the other 30 days.

::: {.keyidea}
**A probability is checked over many cases, not one.** "70% chance of rain" means that on 100 such days, it should rain on about 70. If it does not rain tomorrow, the forecast was not wrong.
:::

The same is true for an AI model. When it says "this alert is 70% likely to be an attack", we can check it the same way: look at many alerts where it said 70%, and count how many were really attacks.

## The rare-event trap

Try this question. A security alarm catches 99% of real attacks, but it also goes off by mistake for 5% of normal activity. Real attacks are rare: about 1 in every 1,000 events. The alarm goes off. What is the chance that it is a real attack?

Most people say about 95%. The correct answer is about **2%**. Even doctors fall into this trap: in a famous 1978 study, most doctors at a top medical college gave the same wrong answer for a medical test [@casscells1978].

![The same puzzle, counted out. Of 100,000 events, 100 are attacks and the detector catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: 4,995 false alarms. When the alarm sounds, you're holding one of 5,094 alerts, and only 99 of them are real.](/figures/ch02/base-rate-tree.pdf){#fig-base-rate-tree}

The easy way to see this is to count real cases instead of using percentages (@fig-base-rate-tree). Take one lakh (100,000) events. Only 100 are attacks, and the alarm catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: that is 4,995 false alarms. So out of 5,094 alarms, only 99 are real, about 2 in 100.

How common something is before we look at any clue is called the **base rate**. Here it is 1 in 1,000. Forgetting it is the most common mistake people make with probability [@gigerenzer1995].

::: {.keyidea}
**When something is rare, most alarms are false.** If only 1 in 1,000 events is an attack, even a 99%-accurate alarm is right only about 2 times in 100. To see this, count it out with 1,00,000 cases instead of using percentages.
:::

The same trap hides inside the word "accuracy". In our example company, a simple rule ("mark an alert as an attack if its threat score is 0.5 or more") is {{< num ch02 accuracy pct >}} accurate. That sounds good, until you notice that a rule that *never* raises any alarm is even more accurate, {{< num ch02 always_benign_acc pct >}}, simply because most alerts are harmless. It is like a weather forecaster in Rajasthan who always says "no rain": right on most days, and useless on the days that matter. So when something is rare, do not judge a model by accuracy. Ask instead: *of the real attacks, how many did it catch?* and *of its alarms, how many were real?*

## How a machine learns a probability

The simplest way a machine can give a probability works like a credit score. It starts with a base number, adds some points for each clue (a bad threat score, a login at 3 a.m., a new country), and then turns the total into a probability between 0% and 100%. This simple model is called **logistic regression**, and banks and hospitals have used it for decades.

How does the machine find the right points for each clue? It learns from past cases where the answer is known. It makes a guess for each case, checks how wrong it was, changes the points a little, and repeats this many thousands of times. The way it measures "how wrong" is designed to reward honest probabilities: a model that says 99% when the truth is 80% gets a worse score than one that says 80%.

::: {.keyidea}
**Every machine learning model learns the same way: guess, check, correct.** It makes a guess, sees how wrong it was, changes its numbers a little, and repeats this millions of times. A small model and ChatGPT both learn like this; only the size is different.
:::

There is one danger to remember. A model can **memorise** its examples instead of learning from them, like a student who memorises last year's question paper and then fails when the questions change. Such a model looks excellent on the cases it studied and does badly on new ones. This is called **overfitting**, and there is only one way to catch it: always test a model on cases it has never seen.

::: {.exercises}
1. A spam filter catches 98% of spam and wrongly flags 1% of normal emails. If only 1% of all emails are spam, what fraction of flagged emails are actually normal? Use counts, as in @fig-base-rate-tree.
:::
